analysis.one_liner: Bans presidential self-pardons, enforces emoluments rules, speeds subpoena enforcement, and makes campaigns report foreign contacts.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late September 2020, the bill went to nine House committees and died there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a series of new legal checks on the presidency and the executive branch. It would ban a president from pardoning himself, require disclosure of materials behind pardons connected to investigations involving the president or his relatives, make it unlawful for a president to take payments or benefits from foreign or domestic governments (including through his private businesses), suspend the statute of limitations on federal crimes committed by a sitting president, and give Congress and ethics offices new tools to enforce those rules. It would also let Congress sue to enforce its subpoenas, limit presidential emergency powers, protect inspectors general and whistleblowers, require campaigns to report foreign contacts, and ban foreign donations of money or candidate information. It never got past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday voters get clearer rules against presidents enriching themselves in office, against self-pardons, and against foreign money or information flowing into campaigns. Federal whistleblowers and inspectors general get stronger protection, and Congress gets faster ways to compel executive officials to testify and turn over documents.

how_it_helps.text: Bans self-pardons outright and extends the federal bribery statute to cover the president, the vice president, and pardons and commutations offered for anything of value, closing a route for selling clemency.

Makes it unlawful for the president to accept emoluments — payments or benefits from foreign or domestic governments, including through his private businesses — lets Congress sue to force disgorgement, and gives the Office of Government Ethics fine and enforcement authority.
Suspends the statute of limitations on any federal offense committed by a sitting president or vice president, so no one can run out the clock on a prosecution by holding office.

Creates an express legal path for the House, Senate, or their committees to sue to enforce congressional subpoenas, with expedited court review and personal penalties for officials who knowingly refuse to comply.
Requires federal campaigns to report foreign contacts and clarifies that foreign donations of money or nonpublic candidate information are banned, plus criminal penalties for violations.

Requires cause for removing inspectors general, strengthens whistleblower protections (including for intelligence community workers), reauthorizes the Merit Systems Protection Board, and increases Hatch Act penalties for political appointees.

Limits presidential emergency declarations by requiring Congress to approve them within about 20 legislative days or they lapse, and requires the Justice Department to publish its legal opinions on budget and spending law and log contacts with the White House about investigations.

analysis.who_pays: The sitting president, his family's private businesses, and senior political appointees bear the direct costs: disclosure requirements, potential fines and disgorgement of foreign payments, limits on emergency powers, and personal legal penalties for defying subpoenas. Political campaigns face new compliance paperwork. Federal agencies face new reporting obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: The president, his businesses, and political appointees

drawbacks.text: The disclosure requirements around pardons connected to investigations involving the president or a relative could reach into prosecutorial files and White House materials, which critics of such proposals argue risks chilling clemency deliberations and the privacy of people who were investigated but not charged.

The subpoena-enforcement title imposes monetary penalties on agency heads personally (paid from their own pay) and declares that privilege claims must be logged and justified, which defenders of executive authority argue oversteps the constitutional separation of powers; the bill text itself acknowledges the underlying appellate court split in the McGahn case.

Voiding a presidential self-pardon and tolling statutes of limitations for sitting presidents raise novel constitutional questions that would likely have been tested in court, since the Constitution does not expressly say whether a president may pardon himself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are structural and long-term: rules that would apply to any president, aimed at self-enrichment, self-pardon, secret foreign money in campaigns, and stonewalling of congressional oversight. The costs fall almost entirely on officeholders and their businesses rather than on ordinary people, though the pardon-disclosure and subpoena-penalty provisions are aggressive enough that courts would likely have been asked to narrow them. On balance it is a strong accountability package whose main weakness is that some provisions are designed for the hardest edge cases.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to nine committees on the day it was introduced, none of them reported it back, and the House never voted on it before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on September 23, 2020, joined by 16 original cosponsors including the chairs of the Judiciary and Oversight committees.

The same day, it was referred to nine House committees: Oversight and Reform, Judiciary, Budget, Transportation and Infrastructure, Rules, Foreign Affairs, Ways and Means, Intelligence, and House Administration; a Transportation subcommittee also got a referral.
92 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
No committee reported the bill and no floor vote ever took place; the last recorded action in the 116th Congress is the original referral sequence, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The presidential practices the bill targeted — self-pardons, foreign payments reaching the president's businesses, unenforced subpoenas, and unreported foreign campaign contacts — stayed as they were, and the officeholders and private interests benefiting from them never had to comply. Ordinary voters got nothing from the process.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officeholders and interests the bill would have regulated

for.name: Rep. Adam Schiff
for.role: Sponsor (D-CA), Chair of the House Intelligence Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 23, 2020, as the lead sponsor of a 17-member original cosponsor group.

for.name: 92 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat and none was a Republican.

against.name: House committee chairs (nine committees of referral)
against.role: Oversight, Judiciary, Budget, Transportation, Rules, Foreign Affairs, Ways and Means, Intelligence, House Administration
against.what_they_did: None of the nine committees to which the bill was referred ever held a hearing, reported it, or scheduled action on it during the roughly three months remaining in the Congress.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote; after the day-one referrals, the action history records no further movement and no vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Senate majority (53 of 100 seats in the 116th Congress)
against.what_they_did: The bill never reached the Senate at all, so no Senate action of any kind occurred while Republicans controlled the floor calendar.

sides.party_line_note: All 93 supporters (the sponsor and 92 cosponsors) were Democrats, no Republican cosponsored, and because the bill never reached a floor vote there is no roll-call record showing any Republican or Democratic support on the merits.

industries.industry: The president's private business interests (e.g., the Trump Organization)
industries.note: The bill bans accepting emoluments through private businesses, requires detailed disclosure of business interests that could produce foreign or state payments, and lets Congress sue for disgorgement. This targeted the then-sitting president's hotels and other ventures that received payments from foreign governments and U.S. officials.

industries.industry: Executive branch political appointees and the White House
industries.note: The bill requires cause to fire inspectors general, increases Hatch Act penalties for political appointees, imposes personal penalties for defying congressional subpoenas, logs DOJ-White House contacts on investigations, and restricts emergency declarations. Every one of these raises the cost of acting on political loyalty instead of law for senior officials.

Campaigns would face new duties — a foreign contacts compliance program and reporting of foreign contacts — backed by criminal penalties. The compliance burden is real, but the rules shield all campaigns from foreign money and stolen information, which most campaigns claim to want.

Agencies face new reporting duties on spending decisions, Antideficiency Act violations, and emergency spending, and must respond to GAO requests within 20 days. The burden falls on agency operations, but the money involved is taxpayer money that Congress, not the president, is supposed to control.
